ReportItem.Name: TLS/SSL Weak Cipher Suites
ReportItem.Details:
Weak TLS/SSL Cipher Suites: (offered via TLS1.2 on port 443):

  • TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_256_CBC_SHA384
  • TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_256_CBC_SHA
  • TLS_DHE_RSA_WITH_AES_256_CBC_SHA256
  • TLS_DHE_RSA_WITH_AES_256_CBC_SHA
  • TLS_DHE_RSA_WITH_CAMELLIA_256_CBC_SHA
ReportItem.Impact:
Weak cipher suites can lead to several serious security implications:

  • Data Exposure: Attackers may decrypt intercepted communications using brute-force attacks against weak encryption algorithms or short key lengths.
  • Padding Oracle Attacks: CBC-mode cipher suites are vulnerable to timing attacks that can reveal plaintext information through padding validation responses, including the POODLE attack against SSLv3 and Lucky Thirteen attacks against TLS implementations.
  • Man-in-the-Middle Attacks: Weak cipher suites facilitate downgrade attacks where attackers force connections to use weaker encryption that can be more easily compromised.
  • Compliance Violations: Use of weak ciphers may violate industry standards and regulatory requirements for data protection.
ReportItem.Description: The remote host supports TLS/SSL cipher suites with weak or insecure properties. Weak cipher suites may use deprecated algorithms, insufficient key lengths, or vulnerable encryption modes that can be exploited by attackers to compromise the confidentiality and integrity of encrypted communications. These vulnerabilities include susceptibility to brute-force attacks, cryptographic weaknesses, and implementation-specific attacks such as padding oracle vulnerabilities in CBC-mode cipher suites.
ReportItem.Recommendation:
Actions to Take:

  1. Disable Weak Cipher Suites: Remove support for all cipher suites using deprecated algorithms, export-grade ciphers, and those with insufficient key lengths (less than 128 bits).
  2. Eliminate CBC-Mode Ciphers: Remove any cipher suite containing CBC (Cipher Block Chaining) mode ciphers, as they are vulnerable to padding oracle attacks including POODLE, Lucky Thirteen, and other timing-based attacks. CBC implementations in TLS have consistently proven susceptible to these vulnerabilities.
  3. Prefer Authenticated Encryption: Configure the server to prioritize authenticated encryption cipher suites such as those using Galois Counter Mode (GCM) or ChaCha20-Poly1305, which provide both confidentiality and authenticity without the vulnerabilities associated with CBC modes.
  4. Enable Forward Secrecy: Configure cipher suites that support Perfect Forward Secrecy (PFS) using Ephemeral Diffie-Hellman (DHE) or Elliptic Curve Ephemeral Diffie-Hellman (ECDHE) key exchange algorithms.
  5. Upgrade TLS Version: Where possible, upgrade to TLS 1.3, which eliminates vulnerable cipher suites by design and only supports authenticated encryption modes.
  6. Regular Security Updates: Implement a process for regularly reviewing and updating cipher suite configurations as cryptographic standards evolve and new vulnerabilities are discovered.

Specific Technical Requirements:

  • Remove cipher suites with key lengths less than 128 bits
  • Disable all CBC-mode cipher suites to prevent padding oracle attacks
  • Eliminate support for RC4, DES, 3DES, and MD5-based cipher suites
  • Configure strong cipher ordering with authenticated encryption prioritized

ReportItem.Name: Content Security Policy (CSP) Not Implemented
ReportItem.Impact: CSP can be used to prevent and/or mitigate attacks that involve content/code injection, such as cross-site scripting/XSS attacks, attacks that require embedding a malicious resource, attacks that involve malicious use of iframes, such as clickjacking attacks, and others.
ReportItem.Description:
Content Security Policy (CSP) is an added layer of security that helps to detect and mitigate certain types of attacks, including Cross Site Scripting (XSS) and data injection attacks.

Content Security Policy (CSP) can be implemented by adding a Content-Security-Policy header. The value of this header is a string containing the policy directives describing your Content Security Policy. To implement CSP, you should define lists of allowed origins for the all of the types of resources that your site utilizes. For example, if you have a simple site that needs to load scripts, stylesheets, and images hosted locally, as well as from the jQuery library from their CDN, the CSP header could look like the following: 

Content-Security-Policy:
    default-src 'self';
    script-src 'self' https://code.jquery.com;


It was detected that your web application doesn't implement Content Security Policy (CSP) as the CSP header is missing from the response. It's recommended to implement Content Security Policy (CSP) into your web application.
ReportItem.Recommendation: It's recommended to implement Content Security Policy (CSP) into your web application. Configuring Content Security Policy involves adding the Content-Security-Policy HTTP header to a web page and giving it values to control resources the user agent is allowed to load for that page.

ReportItem.Name: X-Content-Type-Options (XCTO) Not Implemented
ReportItem.Impact: XCTO header can be used as an additional layer of defense to prevent various attacks, such as Cross-Site Scripting (XSS), Cross-Site Script Inclusion (XSSI), side channel attacks, and others.
ReportItem.Description:
MIME type sniffing is a standard functionality in browsers to find an appropriate way to render data where the HTTP headers sent by the server are either inconclusive or missing.
This allows web browsers to perform MIME-Sniffing on the response body, potentially causing the response body to be interpreted and displayed as a content type other than the intended content type.

X-Content-Type-Options (XCTO) is an HTTP header that can be used to prevent MIME type sniffing, which can help to mitigate certain types of attacks, including Cross Site Scripting (XSS). It also enables Cross-Origin Read Blocking (CORB) for sensitive resources, helping protect against Cross-Site Script Inclusion (XSSI) and side channel attacks.
ReportItem.Recommendation: Add the X-Content-Type-Options header with a value of "nosniff" to inform the browser to trust what the site has sent is the appropriate content-type, and to not attempt "sniffing" the real content-type.
